scenario: AITA for not jumping up and helping my parents bring in the groceries? I'm an adult and I pay rent if that helps. | I'm 33 years old and I've pretty much always lived with my parents. To me there's no shame in it because it's super cheap (they charge me $200, which honestly would be market rate where we live) and it has everything I want and need without the hassle of having to look for a new place to live. We get along most of the time but honestly I just avoid them. Recently the toilet flooded in my bathroom which means they are having to remodel my section of the house so we "run into" each other a lot more than when I used to lock myself in my room most of the time. Well today my parents went to Costco. When they got home I was sitting on the couch playing Apex and my mom asked me to get up and help them bring in groceries. I told her in a minute. I was honestly too into my game to notice that they made several trips back and forth and finally my dad told me to get my ass up. I told him I would in a minute. He said a minute is now and grabbed the controller out of my hand. It turned into a huge shouting match and now they are checking into a hotel and expecting me to have a place to live by Friday (which is basically impossible). Of course they brought up my younger brother who is married with two kids and was just promoted at his job. They have their golden child of course but to throw his shit in my face is bullshit. I mean I guess I could have gotten up and helped them but to me because I pay rent that gives me the privilege to pretty much say no when they ask me for stuff like helping with groceries or yard work. Am I the asshole in this situation?

prediction.raw: **1 (Yes, you're the asshole)** **Why:** - **Basic courtesy and shared responsibility:** Even as an adult paying rent, living in someone else’s home (especially a family member’s) implies mutual respect and shared household duties. $200 rent is *significantly* below market rate in most areas, meaning your parents are subsidizing your living costs. In return, it’s reasonable to expect small contributions like helping with groceries, especially when they’re clearly struggling (multiple trips, heavy loads). - **"In a minute" is not an excuse:** repeatedly saying "in a minute" while continuing to play a game shows dismissiveness. When someone asks for help with physical labor, "in a minute" should mean *immediately*—not a delay that escalates frustration. Your parents were carrying groceries *while you sat idle*, which is inconsiderate. - **"Privilege to say no" is misapplied:** paying rent doesn’t grant you a free pass to refuse basic help. It’s not about " chores vs. rent"—it’s about being a respectful housemate. If you were a roommate (not family), you’d still be expected to pitch in for something as simple as unloading groceries. - **Parents’ overreaction is separate:** while their response ( checking into a hotel, demanding you move by Friday) is harsh and disproportionate, it doesn’t excuse your initial behavior. *You* started the conflict by being uncooperative. - **Brother comparisons are irrelevant:** their " golden child" narrative doesn’t change your responsibility to contribute. Focus on your own actions, not their unfair comparisons. **Fix:** Apologize for being dismissive, offer to help with the remodel (or other tasks), and clarify expectations for future household contributions. Moving out is a separate issue, but *today’s* conflict was your fault for not showing basic respect. **Final verdict:** AITA. You’re the asshole for being inconsiderate and uncooperative when asked to help with a simple, physical task.
